Common words: verbs, qualities & ideas

abandon verb

a person or a place

also desert, forsake, leave behind, leave in the lurch, let down, abandoned

classical

Cic. Q. Fr. 1.3.5: cum amīcī partim dēseruerint mē, partim etiam prōdiderint (Lewis & Short)
Verg. A. 10.600: frātrem nē dēsere frāter (Lewis & Short)

dēserō, dēserere, dēseruī, dēsertum

verb, third conjugation, with the accusative · Conjugation on Wiktionary

abandon, desert, forsake

Leave someone or something one should stand by: friends, an army, a post, a cause. Narrower than relinquere and, from its military use, often implying cowardice (Lewis & Short). Of things, “fail, give out”.

Other words

  • relinquō, relinquere, relīquī, relictum — leave behind, leave

    verb, third conjugation, with the accusative · also used · classical · Ter. Phorm. 1.2.22: mē fīliīs relinquont quasi magistrum (Lewis & Short) · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    The general word for leaving a person or a place behind, which need not blame (Lewis & Short); also “leave over, bequeath”.

  • dēstituō, dēstituere, dēstituī, dēstitūtum — leave in the lurch, let down

    verb, third conjugation, with the accusative · also used · classical · Cic. Rosc. Am. 117: indūxit, dēcēpit, dēstituit, adversāriīs trādidit (Lewis & Short); Phaedr. 5.10: nōn tē dēstituit animus, sed vīrēs meae · Conjugation on Wiktionary

    Leave someone alone when he relies on you. Its first sense is “set down, place” (Livy, Plautus) (Lewis & Short).

Examples

  • cum amīcī partim dēseruerint mē, partim etiam prōdiderint

    since some of my friends have abandoned me and some have even betrayed meCic. Q. Fr. 1.3.5 (Lewis & Short)

  • nōtāsque palūdēs dēserit atque altam suprā volat ardea nūbem

    and the heron leaves its familiar marshes and flies above the high cloudsVerg. G. 1.363–364

  • nōn tē dēstituit animus, sed vīrēs meae

    it was not my courage that let you down, but my strengthPhaedr. 5.10

See also abandon, go, leave me alone!.
